entries.title: Housing Action Illinois sues HUD as Trump administration brands nonprofit 'radical left NGO'
entries.summary: <p>A federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration's efforts to cut roughly $56 million in housing counseling funding — giving Chicago-based Housing Action Illinois and nine other nonprofits across the U.S. some relief.</p><p>The victory comes after the 10 nonprofits sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development on Tuesday for attempting to claw back funding allocated for HUD's Comprehensive Housing Counseling program. The program was created by Congress to provide consumers with first-time homebuyer education classes, foreclosure prevention assistance and other services.</p><p>The Democracy Defenders Fund and Jacobson Lawyers Group filed the lawsuit on behalf of the organizations, which includes the National Urban League, North Carolina Housing Coalition, New Jersey Citizen Action, Housing & Community Development Network of NJ, National CAPACD, Fair Housing Resource Center, Southwest Fresno Community Development Corporation, Somerville Community Corporation and the National Foundation for Debt Management.</p><p>The attorneys filed a temporary restraining order Wednesday, urging the court to extend the deadline for the funds’ allocation. The funds would have expired Wednesday had the court not intervened.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Jia Cobb ruled late Wednesday that suspending the deadline was necessary so the nonprofits and the government could have more time to argue their case.</p><p>“The Court is hesitant to determine whether the government is required to obligate nearly $60 million without the government itself being fully heard on the issue,” Cobb wrote in her decision. “However, the Court is likewise hesitant to allow September 30 to pass such as that Plaintiffs would lose out on significant amounts of funding due to allegedly unconstitutional actions.”</p><p>The nonprofits said in their <a class="Link" href="https://www.democracydefendersfund.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/092926_DDF-Complaint-National-Urban-League.pdf" target="_blank" >complaint</a> that the funds were illegally being withheld because they expressed views rejected by the Trump administration, violating First Amendment protections. And "to punish grantees," President Donald Trump used a pocket rescission to block congresionally appropriated funds. </p><p>In a news release last week announcing the rescission package, the White House claimed a number of nonprofits receiving HUD funds were peddling diversity, equity and inclusion practices and discriminating against people based on their race.</p><p>The release went on to call out Housing Action Illinois, saying the nonprofit was “a radical left NGO [nongovernmental organization] that believes ‘housing is a human right,’ and is committed to ‘advancing equitable community development and affirmatively furthering racial justice.’” The rescission included $1.5 million that was allocated to Housing Action Illinois.</p><p>The government opposed Cobb's suspension, arguing the court doesn’t have the power to override deadlines established by Congress. </p><p>Both parties will have a chance to present their case later this month, after the government submits a more detailed response to the nonprofits’ lawsuit.</p><p>Sharon Legenza, executive director of Housing Action Illinois, said the nonprofit was “very relieved” the temporary restraining order was granted. Keeping the funds in play means the nonprofits can continue to provide housing counseling support, and they may get reimbursed for services dating back to October 2025 — the start of the federal government’s fiscal year.</p><p>The 40-year-old nonprofit has done a “wide variety” of work to help people access safe and quality homes, Legenza said. </p><p>In fiscal year 2024, Housing Action Illinois’ housing counseling network served more than 12,500 households, according to a court declaration written by David Young, the nonprofit's director of capacity building. Almost 1,400 households that were served purchased their first home, and nearly 430 households evaded or resolved a mortgage default. In 2025, more than 750 participants from across the nation attended Housing Action Illinois’ housing counseling training, according to Young.</p><p>As part of its work, the group serves as an intermediary for HUD’s Comprehensive Housing Counseling program. It applies for the funding, then doles it out as subgrants among its 38 subgrantees.</p><p>Housing Action Illinois’ subgrantees work across eight states and Washington, D.C., to provide housing services to residents, according to Legenza.</p><p>“As we think about … inflation and just the increased cost of housing generally, more and more people are feeling stretched, and more and more people are looking to get assistance to help them figure out how are they going to be able to maintain their housing,” she said. “That's what housing counseling agencies do.”</p>

entries.title: Man, 63, charged with fatally shooting his sister in Auburn Gresham, police report says
entries.summary: <p>A man faces murder charges after an argument apparently led him to fatally shoot his older sister Wednesday afternoon in the Auburn Gresham neighborhood, according to a Chicago police report. </p><p>Randy Washington, 63, was arguing with Dorothy Washington, his 70-year-old sister, inside a residence in the 1900 block of West 83rd Street at 3:18 p.m., when he allegedly shot her in the chest, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. </p><p>Washington, who was arrested at the scene, was charged with one felony count of first-degree murder and is scheduled to appear in court Friday.</p><p>A sibling of the two was on the scene and spoke to police, the report said. </p><p>Dorothy Washington was pronounced dead at 3:25 p.m., according to the Cook County medical examiner's office. <br></p>

entries.title: White Sox ready for ALDS showdown with Guardians that will be 'one to remember'
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> won their season series (seven games to six) against the division rival Guardians. But couldn’t hold them off in a late-September three-game set at Cleveland, or the American League Central standings as the Guardians won 24 of their last 34 games.</p><p>“It’s going to be one to remember,” reliever <b>Grant Taylor</b> said to the Sun-Times about this weekend’s ALDS matchup. “We’re going to go in and try to win two games at their place.”</p><p>It’s a playoff showdown that feels inevitable because the regular-season battle feels unresolved. Are the standings flipped if the fly ball Guardians infielder<b> Brayan Rocchio</b> lifted off Taylor found <b>Sam Antonacci</b>’s glove? Or was the level of baseball Cleveland reached down the stretch simply a cut above the rest of the division?</p><p>“We can beat Cleveland,” said general manager <b>Chris Getz</b>. “We’ve proven that we can. But they are definitely a team that’s been here before, and we respect them.”</p><p>The sides have disparate strengths.</p><p>The Sox followed up leading the AL in runs scored by chasing two Astros starters before they could complete the first inning, whereas the Guardians’ offense finished 11th, even with a late-season kick.</p><p>The Guardians flaunt a deep rotation and will throw likely AL Cy Young finalist <b>Parker Messick</b> in Game 1, followed by league strikeout leader <b>Gavin Williams</b> in Game 2. The Sox’ reliance on their bullpen will be strained over a best-of-five series and manager <b>Will Venable</b> laughed at the idea of having their Game 1 starter determined during Wednesday’s postgame celebration.</p><p>As much as the Sox celebrated guaranteeing a home playoff game by reaching this round, they will need to win at Progressive Field to advance, where they dropped four of seven in the regular season. It’s always the slimmest margin between these two.</p><p>But where the White Sox’ strong first half was reliant on dominance at home to offset struggles on the road, a postseason triumph in Houston has them feeling differently.</p><p>“All we need is our dugout,” said shortstop <b>Colson Montgomery</b>. “We love our fans and we love everyone that comes and travels and supports us. But it's about our dugout. We need each other and believe in each other.”</p><h3><b>Hicks on a heater</b></h3><p>Houston native <b>Jordan Hicks </b>was letter-perfect pitching in his hometown, retiring all 10 Astros he faced over his two Wild Card series appearances, striking out four.</p><p>After a rocky start to the year, Hicks raised his arm slot while sidelined with a lat strain, and found it restored the riding action on his four-seam fastball. His sinker also sinks less in turn, but forcing hitters to guess between two different types of triple-digit fastballs offset the loss.</p><p>Moreover, the newfound consistency of his delivery at this release point has made him a reliable option.</p><p>“I'm in a better position just throwing strikes at 100 to 102 mph versus trying to reach back for 103, 104 mph and then kind of spraying it a little bit, losing the feel,” Hicks said.</p><p>Being able to dial down to <i>just</i> 102 mph is a good place to be.</p><h3><b>ABS wizardry</b></h3><p>The White Sox preach being aggressive on challenges with the automated ball and strikes system (ABS), and are prouder of leading MLB in challenge rate than worried about being worst in success rate.</p><p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b> balanced both in Houston, going 5-for-5 on challenges over two games.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/01/white-sox-manager-will-venable-doesnt-fear-mistakes-and-his-team-is-fearless-in-return" >White Sox manager Will Venable doesn’t fear mistakes, and his team is fearless in return</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox manager Will Venable doesn't fear mistakes, and his team is fearless in return
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> manager Will Venable doesn’t always say the right thing.</p><p>“Speaking is not really my thing as far as literally getting words out and effectively communicating,” Venable told the Sun-Times. “I say ‘um’ all the time. Sometimes I say words and I'm like, ‘Damn, that didn't come out right.’”</p><p>The second-year skipper has a book of tongue twisters he’ll return to for practice. As he entered into coaching, he recalls reaching out to his friend, A’s broadcaster Jenny Cavnar for help on his public speaking, and credits her for giving him opportunities to practice in radio interviews.</p><p>Even stories from teammates about times he showed leadership during his playing days described Venable as more of an effective communicator, aided by the gravitas that his work ethic lent him, rather than an eager one. Working a job defined by communication across the endless different branches of an MLB organization required an evolution, but still reflects someone who doesn’t talk for the sake of talking.</p><p>“We're kids when we play this game, and he's a fully grown, mature adult doing this now,” said Sox field coordinator Chris Denorfia, who played with Venable on the Padres. “[His communication style] is the same, but it's more finely-tuned. He extends that into the coaching room. He wants all of our messages to be short, to the point, no fluff.”</p><p>A byproduct that’s more intentional with time is the lack of obfuscation. Venable doesn’t mince words in a postgame interview when one of his many non-traditional, metric-guided moves doesn’t pan out. He wants all his communication that way.</p><p>“The first layer is me talking about how I messed up, right, that takes some heat off of [the players],” Venable said. “The second part is everyone is going to make mistakes, right? I'm going to make mistakes, players are going to make mistakes, everyone is going to make mistakes. We need to have an environment where it's okay to make mistakes, we're not going to crumble because we make mistakes. We're going to make mistakes the right way. You're going to be accountable to it.”</p><p>For a White Sox roster asked constantly about their lack of experience, the idea that growing pains or protracted struggles are inevitable, rather than a source of shame, is brought up a lot. As the Sox’ arrive to October, they’ve felt the absence of an overbearing presence.</p><p>“Will's the man,” said shortstop Colson Montgomery. “Having a manager like that where you can kind of turn off the baseball player and turn on just being like, a man, like bros talking pretty much. So I think that's kind of what I've appreciated a lot about him. His communication is great.”</p><p>“He's a voice to be heard and he says what he needs to say when there's something that we need to address,” said starter Sean Burke. “But I think, honestly, one of his best traits is he let's us be a lot.”</p><p>In early September, Venable said few members of his team had experienced the abasement of individual priorities that postseason baseball requires, but he assumed they’d handle it well.</p><p>In a Wild Card Series sweep in Houston, his defacto No. 3 starter Anthony Kay agreed to a bullpen assignment to get the biggest outs of the clinching game, Grant Taylor affirmed he was good for a Game 1 ninth inning that took him to a career-high 54 pitches, and Burke went viral for a quote to the Sun-Times asserting his commitment to the team in such intense terms that he had to affirm he does have a real family, beyond just his White Sox teammates.</p><p>“It’s easier to put your body on the line when you’ve got guys like this around you,” Taylor said postgame Wednesday, after confirming he wasn’t actually available to pitch in Game 2.</p><p>In this environment, the bigger risk is Venable’s players offering him more than they can actually handle. He hopes he’s established it’s good to be honest.</p><p></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/01/white-sox-ready-for-alds-showdown-with-guardians-that-will-be-one-to-remember" >White Sox ready for ALDS showdown with Guardians that will be ‘one to remember’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: 'Broadview Six' judge wants to put prosecutors under oath, keeps contempt charges on the table
entries.summary: <p>When federal prosecutors in Chicago assured a judge last spring<b> </b>they’d had no contact with the White House or top Justice Department officials about their pursuit of six Operation Midway Blitz protesters, U.S. District Judge April Perry<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/04/07/broadview-ice-kat-abughazaleh-chicago-midway-blitz" target="_blank" ><u>took them at their word</u></a>.</p><p>Those days are clearly over.</p><p>Rather, in a remarkable turn-the-tables moment that underscores the damage done to the feds’ credibility here, Perry<b> </b>concluded Thursday<b> </b>that<b> </b>further<b> </b>“under oath”<b> </b>fact-finding<b> </b>is needed in the tainted case of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>“Broadview Six”</u></a> — leaving open the possibility that she’ll name a special prosecutor to investigate U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>and others.</p><p>She did so at the end of an hourlong hearing<b> </b>in which she asked an attorney for Boutros’ office, point-blank, whether any of the prosecutors who worked on the politically charged case would invoke their Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.</p><p>He said he didn’t know.</p><p>Eventually, Perry told the lawyers, The judge also<b> </b>indicated<b> </b>Mecklenburg<b> </b>had excused grand jurors who disagreed with the feds’ case, a claim Mecklenburg denies.</p><p>Mecklenburg retired<b> </b>from the Justice Department<b> </b>last week <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/25/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg" target="_blank" ><u>in order to defend herself</u></a>.</p><p>Perry said she found “most problematic”<b> </b>the fact that the apparent misconduct was redacted out of transcripts<b> </b>initially given to her by Boutros’ office. The redactions were made after<b> </b>Mecklenburg withdrew from the case.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/09/25/broadview-six-boutros-mecklenburg" >‘Broadview Six’ prosecutor slams Boutros in resignation letter, saying he pushed doomed felony charges</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The prosecutors who remained – and nearly took it to trial – were<b> </b>William<b> </b>Hogan, Matthew<b> </b>Skiba<b> </b>and<b> </b>Andres<b> </b>Almendarez. During Thursday’s hearing, Boutros’ office was represented by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Maxwell<b> </b>Lisy<b> </b>and<b> </b>Nathaniel<b> </b>Whalen.</p><p>It wasn’t long ago that Chicago’s U.S. attorney’s office was considered one of the top tier in the nation. Perry <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/17/broadview-six-judge-april-perry-trump-vance" target="_blank" ><u>once served in the office</u></a> and helped prosecute Jon<b> </b>Burge, the late Chicago police commander tied to torture claims who was ultimately convicted of perjury.</p><p>President Joe Biden nominated<b> </b>Perry<b> </b>in 2023 to serve as Chicago’s top federal prosecutor. JD Vance, who is now vice president.</p><p>Boutros was initially named U.S. attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/03/28/former-prosecutor-andrew-boutros-named-chicagos-interim-u-s-attorney" target="_blank" ><u>on a temporary basis</u></a> by then-Attorney General Pam<b> </b>Bondi<b> </b>in April 2025. entries.title: Jeanne Gang and a North Lawndale community garden among the honorees at architecture's Designight 2026
entries.summary: <p>The Humboldt Park Health Wellness Center — with its iridescent green and blue cladding, designed to match the colors of the Caribbean Sea — is among the buildings that took top honors Thursday at the AIA Chicago's Designight 2026 awards ceremony.</p><p>Chicago firm Studio Gang, led by Aqua Tower architect Jeanne Gang, was also given the architecture organization's 2026 Firm Award, which recognizes a firm's body of work over the last 10 years.</p><p>The awards were among 52 projects that were recognized at the Chicago chapter of the American Institute of Architects' yearly gala, held at the Harris Theater for Music and Dance in Millennium Park.</p><p>Long-dubbed the "Oscars of Chicago architecture," Designight recognizes the best projects by local architects.</p><p>The Humboldt Park Health Wellness Center, 2933 W. Division St., snagged the Design Excellence Honor Award in the medium-sized firm subcategory.</p><p>Built for Humboldt Park Health, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/02/28/humboldt-park-wellness-center-puerto-rican-culture-architecture-lee-bey" target="_blank" >the $30 million center</a> by the firm JGMA was lauded for a design that reflects Humboldt Park's Puerto Rican heritage.</p><p>With Studio Gang, the awards jury praised the firm's "impact and legacy [that] extends well beyond individual projects, encompassing global influence on sustainable design, public engagement, and the evolution of architectural practice."</p><p>The celebrated firm is known for a portfolio of work that includes Lakeshore East skyscrapers Aqua Tower and the St. Regis, as well as smaller projects like the Nature Boardwalk at Lincoln Park Zoo and the Lavezzorio Community Center in Auburn Gresham.</p><div entries.title: With White Sox-Guardians series scheduled to start in daylight, Blackout Game might be tough
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox can have another Blackout Game, but it might have to start in daylight.</p><p>MLB released the entire schedule for the divisional round of the playoffs Thursday. Games 3 and 4 of the Sox' series against the Guardians at Rate Field are scheduled for 3 p.m. Wednesday and 4 next Thursday, respectively. That doesn't make for prime blackout conditions, at least not until sunset around 6:30. If Game 4 is the only game that day, it will start at 7, offering some hope.</p><p>Games 1 and 2 in Cleveland are set for noon Saturday and 4 p.m. Monday, respectively. If necessary, Game 5 is scheduled for 4 p.m. Oct. 10 in Cleveland. If it's the only Game 5 that day, it will start at 7. All games will air on TBS and truTV and streaming service HBO Max. Alex Faust, analyst Ron Darling and reporter Lauren Jbara will call it.</p><p>Sox-Guardians games are scheduled to be the first games each day they're played, a sure sign that the league and networks have more desirable games later. The Rays-Yankees series, for example, has Games 2-5 scheduled for prime time at 7 p.m.</p><p>The Sox' first Blackout Game was the tiebreaker against the Twins for the 2008 American League Central title. Jim Thome's solo home run in the seventh inning was the only run of the game. The Sox brought the blackout back for Game 3 of the 2021 AL Division Series against the Astros, igniting a raucous crowd that saw the Sox win 12-6. <br></p>

entries.title: NFL commissioner Roger Goodell visits Illinois again for more Bears stadium talks with Gov. JB Pritzker
entries.summary: <p>Illinois is still moving the chains in stadium talks to keep the Bears from jumping the state line to Indiana, officials said Thursday.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker met with NFL commissioner Roger Goodell, Bears minority owner Pat Ryan and the top legislative leaders who have been wrangling for several years over the property tax incentives the team is seeking to break ground in Arlington Heights.</p><p>It was Goodell’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/14/bears-stadium-hammond-arlington-heights-report-roger-goodell-met-illinois-lawmakers-nfl-commissioner" target="_blank" ><u>second meeting</u></a> in as many months with Illinois officials, while Ryan — who bankrolled his namesake stadium opening later this week at <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/college-sports/2026/10/01/northwestern-ryan-field-penn-state-wildcats-nittany-lions-evanston-friday-college-football" target="_blank" ><u>Northwestern University</u></a> — takes a more active role in negotiations with the state over Bears president Kevin Warren, who hasn’t made inroads in Springfield.</p><p>The conversation, held in Chicago, also included Illinois House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch and the Capitol’s top stadium negotiators, South Side state Sen. Bill Cunningham and downtown state Rep. Kam Buckner.</p><p>Pritzker’s office noted they’ve “remained in conversation with the Bears about their plans in Illinois throughout the summer,” since the team announced in June that they were shifting focus to Hammond, Indiana.</p><p>Sources familiar with Thursday’s discussion suggested there was no major breakthrough, but some optimism that common ground could be found before lawmakers return to Springfield in mid-November for the fall veto session. Further meetings are expected this month.</p><p>"The Governor and General Assembly leadership were glad to participate in a productive meeting focused on keeping the Bears in Illinois and protecting taxpayers,” Pritzker’s office said in a press release announcing the meeting.</p><p>"The NFL appreciated the opportunity to meet with Gov. Pritzker and legislative leaders today,” NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy said in a statement. “Timely action is essential as the Bears work to find a long-term stadium solution for the club and their fans."</p><p>A Bears spokesman had no additional comment.</p><p>Hoosier lawmakers have rolled out <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/02/26/bears-stadium-hammond-indiana-hammong-senate-passes-bill-27-arlington-heights-george-mccaaskey-kevin-warren-nfl" target="_blank" ><u>the red carpet</u></a> for the Bears with legislation that would pump upwards of a billion taxpayer dollars into a new stadium.</p><p>Earlier this year, the Illinois House passed a bill that would allow the Bears to negotiate a discounted payment in lieu of taxes with local taxing bodies, earning critical support from Chicago Democrats because it would’ve shared proceeds with homeowners as property tax rebates — but those returns were deemed “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/04/bears-stadium-property-tax-relief-pritzker-negligible" target="_blank" ><u>negligible</u></a>.”</p><p>The Illinois Senate passed a separate bill that would allow municipalities to create their own stadium authorities to negotiate with teams, but it crumbled in the waning hours of spring session <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium/2026/05/31/bears-stadium-bill-springfield-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana" target="_blank" ><u>without a vote in the other chamber</u></a>.</p><p>The Bears turned their noses at both measures, but haven’t spelled out what they want from the state beyond “property tax certainty.”</p><p>Ryan, a billionaire with a 10% stake in the team, has helped improve the tenor of discussions that had stagnated between Illinois officials and Halas Hall, according to sources familiar with the talks.</p><p>Goodell has toured the potential stadium sites in Arlington Heights and Hammond. Without stating a preference, he has publicly urged the Bears to come to a resolution “soon” — but Illinois sources are taking his visits as an indication that the league thinks the team is better off in its original state.</p><p>The Bears have committed to putting $2 billion into a new stadium wherever they end up. They’re under lease at Soldier Field until 2033.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sun-Times sports reporter Pat Finley</i></p>

entries.title: McHenry man sentenced to 12 years for battering infant son
entries.summary: <p>A McHenry man was sentenced to 12 years in prison for battering his then-infant son four years ago, according to the McHenry County state’s attorney’s office.</p><p>DeShawn M. Wilson, 28, pleaded guilty to a charge of aggravated battery to a child.</p><p>On July 17, 2022, paramedics responded to a call about an unresponsive infant, who was initially taken to Northwestern Medicine McHenry Hospital before being airlifted to Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital to treat a severe brain injury that required emergency surgery, prosecutors said.</p><p>Wilson had been caring for the 4-month-old child while his mother was at work, and admitted to police he had bounced and shaken the baby in an attempt to get him to sleep.</p><p>“This resolution holds Wilson accountable for the devastating and lasting injuries he caused his infant son,” McHenry County State’s Attorney Randi Freese said in a statement. “Our hope is that [the child’s family] can now move forward with their full attention where it belongs — on this child, his continued care, and his well-being.”</p>

entries.title: The dive after five overtimes: Lake View beats Von Steuben in rain-soaked thriller
entries.summary: <p>Early Thursday evening, everyone at Lane Stadium would have agreed that Lake View vs. Von Steuben was a crucial White North game.</p><p>When it finally ended at nearly 11 p.m., after five overtimes, the game had become much more.</p><p>“You are going to remember this night for the rest of your lives,” Lake View coach Kipp Duplechine told his team after their 36-34 victory.</p><p>Outside the stadium, a large Von Steuben player sobbed as his much smaller father hugged and consoled him, saying, “Sometimes that is how life is going to go.”</p><p>Both teams left everything on the field, battling each other and the constant rain. There were 13 fumbles. Lake View was 0-for-7 passing, and Von Steuben was 3-for-14.</p><p>Several large puddles lined the sideline, and some of the Wildcats dived into them to celebrate the win.</p><p>“It was hard,” Lake View running back Kaleb Lovett said. “I lost my voice I was yelling so much. I just thought of my coach’s voice telling me to keep going. I didn’t want to disappoint him.”</p><p>Lovett scored the game-winning two-point conversion after his five-yard, game-tying TD in the fifth overtime.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> entries.title: Blackhawks already facing adversity after blowout loss to Mammoth
entries.summary: <p>SALT LAKE CITY — Any hopes that the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks" target="_blank" >Blackhawks</a>' first-game struggles were largely due to quality of opponent were dashed Thursday.</p><p>In a 6-0 blowout loss against a solid but probably not elite Mammoth team, the Hawks looked even more discombobulated than they did <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/09/30/blackhawks-golden-knights-nhl-season-opener-patrick-kane" >Tuesday</a>.</p><p>It remains foolish to jump to conclusions after just two games (out of 84). The Sharks lost their first six games last season before becoming one of the NHL's most-improved teams, after all.</p><p>But if one did jump to conclusions now, they would likely be along these lines: the Hawks are the worst team of all time, they'll never make the playoffs again and perhaps the apocalypse is imminent.</p><p>That's how atrocious these two games have been.</p><p>"Obviously, [we] haven't seen our best hockey yet, by far," a tight-lipped Frank Nazar said. "So [we'll] continue to focus on the process and keep working towards that, because you know it's going to come."</p><p>Said a more loquacious Ian Cole: "I'm sure we're going to have a lot of conversations going forward here. We have a long flight ahead of us [to Buffalo]. I'm sure they'll be broached on that. It's not good enough. We think that we're a much better team than this."</p><p>The Hawks were consistently incapable of exiting their defensive zone Thursday, either because the Mammoth anticipated and intercepted their passes or because they missed their mark or whiffed on the puck entirely. </p><p>Coach Jeff Blashill said the Hawks made decisions "too slow," which was evident.</p><p>Two periods in, the Mammoth held an absurd 31-8 advantage in scoring chances (including 12-0 in high-danger chances). The Hawks' better third period was essentially irrelevant.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Mammoth goal: Anders Lee tips in a shot from the point. 4-0. <a href="https://t.co/drTt7D2azc">pic.twitter.com/drTt7D2azc</a></p>— BHF (@BlackhawksFocus) <a href="https://x.com/BlackhawksFocus/status/2105855940670939528?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">October 2, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Bowen Byram, acquired to be the Hawks' new premier defenseman, was one of many players who especially struggled. </p><p>After Byram's pairing with Alex Vlasic was outshot 12-1 and conceded two goals in the first half of the game, Blashill moved him back to his natural left side, pairing him with Artyom Levshunov. The forward lines were also thoroughly shuffled, continuing this week's trend.</p><p>"I have tons of belief in these guys," Blashill said. "I said it when I took the job: 'You stay steady on the rudder.' Man, this is two games. ... Yes, we have urgency to go play a good hockey game on Saturday. But my focus is on us continuing to get better as a group. That doesn’t change."</p><h3><b>Bedard watch</b></h3><p>As other Blackhawks trickled off the ice following practice Wednesday, Connor Bedard was getting dressed to go on the ice by himself.</p><p>Bedard has been on the ice a lot lately, which seems like a good sign. But general manager Kyle Davidson isn't willing to commit yet to Bedard returning sooner than November, as originally estimated.</p><p>"We're just operating off the initial timeline," Davidson said Tuesday. "All along, we were going to find out new information, if anything, probably in October. Until we have that..."</p><h3><b>Energy management</b></h3><p>The Hawks held their usual pre-game meetings but didn't hold a morning skate Thursday.</p><p>It sounded like they might try minimizing morning skates this season, although the way things played out Thursday might change their minds.</p><p>"We just felt like, from an energy-management standpoint, we didn't want certain guys on the ice," Blashill said before the game. "And those guys were probably going on the ice if we gave them the option.</p><p>"It's one of the hard challenges of coaching in this league, trying to find that balance of when to practice, when to conserve energy. If you never practice, you lose your habits and probably your structure. If you practice all the time, you probably play tired. There's no easy solution to it."</p>

entries.title: Historic Avalon Regal Theater in play for $250,000 in repair funds
entries.summary: <p>The Avalon Regal Theater — the South Side's Moorish Revival jewel box that fell into decay after closing 16 years ago — is in line to get a $249,500 city grant to help fix up the landmark venue, the Chicago Department of Planning and Development announced Friday.</p><p>The cash from the agency's Adopt-A-Landmark Fund would help pay for critical masonry repairs and rebuild the exposed brick substructure of a tower on the northwest corner of the 99-year-old theater at 1645 E. 79th St.</p><p>Also covered under the grant would be the selective removal and resetting of displaced masonry, isolated repointing, temporary supplemental stabilization of the building and the isolated repairs on the theater's front facade, the department said.</p><p>The theater is among three projects recommended for a total of $666,400 in repair funding under the Adopt-A-Landmark program.
